newsitem.title: ABU DHABI: Mideast crude exporters face tough Western markets.
newsitem.headline: Mideast crude exporters face tough Western markets.

text.p: Middle East oil exporters face tougher competition in Western crude markets because of sharply increasing supplies from Atlantic basin producers, a leading oil industry economist said on Monday.

Combined crude output from the Americas, west and north Africa, Central Asian republics and the North Sea is projected to rise by a combined 6.6 million barrels per day (bpd) between 1995-2000, Keith Hamm, chairman of UK analysts Petroleum Economics Ltd told delegates at a conference in Abu Dhabi.

This is more than the approximately six million bpd of crude that Middle East exporters sell in west of Suez markets and would result in these exporters having to sell at prices consistently lower than those achievable in Asian markets.

"The Middle East can continue to supply (the Atlantic basin) but at a competitive price...less than east of Suez (prices)," said Hamm, noting Saudi Arabian Arab Light crude prices in western markets were already consistently below eastern prices.
"(Regional premiums) previously used to fluctuate between east and west...A two-tier market now exists...This premium will get bigger and bigger," Hamm said.
Middle East oil exporters, led by Saudi Arabia and Iran, price their crudes on premiums or discounts to different benchmark crudes for east and west of Suez markets.
These differentiatls are changed either on a monthly or quarterly basis by state-owned producers to take account of demand changes in east or western markets.

The main increase in Atlantic basin crude output -- 4.55 million bpd of heavy and/or sour crudes which is the typical Middle East export grade -- would come from Venezuela, Brazil, Central Asian and the North Sea, Hamm said.
Venezuela alone would lift output by 850,000 bpd to 3.5 million bpd in the year 2000 fron 1995 levels, all of which would be sour -- comparable to Middle East crudes.
A further 2.05 million bpd of light sweet crude, led by Nigeria and Colombia, would be pumped by the year 2000.
Despite a projected 3.5 million bpd increase in Atlantic basin crude runs in 1995-2000 to keep up with rising demand, excess supply in the basin would be 3.1 million bpd because of higher output.
